title: The first concert, at the London Palladium
summary: Dance recalls the band's first concert-hall performance; Cootie recalls playing theaters as an act and enjoys audiences who understand jazz.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: That's it, yeah. Well, listen, if I remember correctly, that first trip to England was the first time the band had ever gave a concert. I think -- you were playing a theater or something. I may be wrong on this, Cootie, but I remember that you had to give a Sunday afternoon concert, in a concert hall. And that's when Constant Lambert was there, the big classical composer, and so on. And did -- you know, he wrote a lot of wonderful things about the band and about Duke as a composer. And I think that was the first time that the band got up on stage and performed as a concert. Do you remember that?
I can't remember it, you know. Too clearly.
No.
But we had been playing theaters, and theaters are similar to concert.
Yeah. That's right. But not -- but in

those days, to play a theater, you're playing a show. And you've got it routined as a show, you know. You have an opener, and you feature this and that and the other thing, and you end up with a -- you know, you close the show with something and so on.
Not in that other period.
No? Tell me about it.
When we played the Palace Theater, we was an act.
Oh, you were part of the show that was at the theater.
That's right.
What would you have, about 35 minutes, do you think?
Yeah. And we played our music.
Yeah.
All around New York we had played theaters. And we played an act, with our music.
But you would close the bill?
Yeah.
You did close it.
We were the stars.
Yeah.
On the show.
Yeah.
We played all the theaters that was open in New York, and around.
Yeah. And then you always had to come back and play a couple of encores.
Yeah.
Because you were closing the bill.
That's right.

Yeah. Well, that's really what I mean, in a way, Cootie. Because -- so, as you say, it was an act, and it was the last act on the bill. And if I remember rightly, you know, there was quite a lot of things written by the critics and by some of the serious critics in the London press, and an arrangement was made to play an actual concert on a concert stage, in a concert hall.
I recall that now.
You remember it?
Yeah. I remember it now.
It was the first time you ever did it.
Yeah.
The band ever did that. And it was very, very thrilling. And the people knew exactly what they were listening to, and what they were hearing, and it was -- you had an absolute ovation. Remember?
Uh-huh.
I think Jack Hylton arranged it or something.
You know, made it possible. Because it was a last minute thing.

Well, I'll tell you one thing. It's a pleasure to play for people that understand your music and understand what you're doing. Now, sometimes you play here in America, and the people don't understand your music and what you're doing. Because they don't know jazz. They don't know nothing about jazz, some people that come to concerts. And some of the universities and things we played, some of them have never heard of Duke Ellington. You know.
You mean the younger generation today.
The younger generation. Yeah.
Yeah.
They don't know nothing about jazz.
Yeah.
And it's kind of hard to play to an audience, you know, that don't know nothing about jazz.
Yeah.
And so it's a pleasure to play in Europe.
Yeah.
All over Europe.
Yeah.
And people know all about jazz.
